Tree Decomposition of Product and Nest Graphs for
Assortment Optimization under the Generalized Nested Logit Model

Yuheng Wang1, Paat Rusmevichientong2, Huseyin Topaloglu3,
Abstract

The generalized nested logit model extends the nested logit model by allowing each product to belong to multiple nests. The overlapping nests in the generalized nested logit model can capture complex substitution patterns, and the model has found applications in many areas. We study the assortment optimization problem under the generalized nested logit model and prove that it is NP-hard when there are only two nests or when any two distinct nests have at most one product in common. Motivated by these complexity results, we introduce novel concepts of product and nest graphs that capture which products are included in which nests. We use the tree decompositions of the graphs to characterize when the assortment optimization problem admits efficient solution methods. When the treewidth of a product graph is bounded, the assortment optimization problem can be solved in polynomial time. If the treewidth of the product graph is unbounded but the treewidth of the nest graph is bounded, then there exists a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. These results represent the first polynomial-time algorithms for assortment optimization under the generalized nested logit model. Our numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the generalized nested logit model provides a better fit to the data than many existing models in the literature.

keywords
Generalized nested logit model, assortment optimization, polynomial-time algorithms

1 Introduction

Discrete choice models have been widely used in operations management to capture how customers choose among alternatives and to represent the demand process. The multinomial logit model is one of the most commonly used discrete choice models; it assumes that a customer assigns independent Gumbel-distributed utilities to each product and chooses the product with the highest utility. The nested logit model generalizes the multinomial logit model by partitioning the set of products into disjoint nests and allows utilities of products within the same nest to be correlated, but the utilities of products in different nests are independent. The generalized nested logit model, also called the cross-nested logit model in the literature, extends the nested logit model by allowing overlapping nests, so that each product can belong to multiple nests, enabling it to capture complex correlation patterns among the product utilities.

Researchers have recognized that the generalized nested logit model can capture more complex substitution patterns than the multinomial logit or nested logit models, and they have applied it to modeling customer choices in a variety of applications. Despite the abundant literature on the applications of generalized nested logit models, there are hardly any papers on operational decisions under this model. In this paper, we study assortment optimization under the generalized nested logit model. Under this model, a customer first chooses among the nests or the outside option. If the customer chooses a nest, she will choose one of the products in that nest. Below is a summary of our contributions.

New complexity results:

Davis et al. (2014) consider the nested logit model, which is a special case of the generalized nested logit in which the nests are disjoint, and prove that the corresponding assortment optimization problem can be solved in polynomial time via linear programming. Prior to our work, it was unknown whether the assortment optimization problem under the generalized nested logit model with overlapping nests is tractable. Our paper settles this question. In contrast to the nested logit model, Theorem 2.1 shows that the assortment optimization problem under the generalized nested logit model is NP-hard. The proof of Theorem 2.1 considers the setting with two nests, each of which contains multiple overlapping products. Theorem 2.2 further shows that the problem remains NP-hard if any two distinct nests share at most one product. We later show that both of these instances admit fully polynomial-time approximation schemes.

Because of its complexity, a common heuristic for solving the assortment optimization problem under the generalized nested logit model is to convert it into the problem of finding a fixed point of some nonincreasing function F:ℝ+→ℝ+F:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}. The challenge here is that for each z∈ℝ+z\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, evaluating the function F⁡(z)F(z) requires solving a high-dimensional combinatorial optimization problem (Zhang et al. 2025). For the special case of the nested logit model, computing F⁡(z)F(z) can be done efficiently via linear programs (Davis et al. 2014). For the generalized nested logit model, however, computing F⁡(z)F(z) is much more difficult. In Theorem 3.7, we prove that it is NP-hard to approximate the value of F⁡(z)F(z) to within any constant factor. This worst-case complexity result is surprising and raises the question of how to identify tractable instances of generalized nested logit models.

Using tree decomposition of product and nest graphs for assortment optimization:

In Section 3, we introduce novel concepts of product and nest graphs. A product graph is an undirected graph in which each vertex corresponds to a product, and there is an edge between two products if they share a common nest. Analogously, a nest graph is an undirected graph in which each vertex corresponds to a nest, and there is an edge between two nests if the two nests share at least one product in common. The edges of these graphs capture how often products appear together and how often nests share common products. Tree decompositions of product and nest graphs give rise to a partition of vertices (Lemma 3.4), and we can use the treewidth — a fundamental concept in graph theory and graph algorithms that measures how far a graph is from a tree — to identify instances where the assortment optimization problem can be solved in polynomial time or approximated with arbitrary accuracy. The connection between the complexity of assortment optimization and the treewidths of product and nest graphs is surprising. Although there is a large literature on using tree decompositions to design algorithms and on using treewidth to characterize the algorithms’ running times, to our knowledge, this is the first paper to show how tree decomposition can be applied to assortment optimization under the generalized nested logit model.

A polynomial-time algorithm for product graphs with bounded treewidths:

In Section 4, we show that when the product graph admits a bounded treewidth that is independent of the number of products or nests, then we can use the tree decomposition to design a polynomial-time dynamic programming algorithm to compute an optimal assortment. To design our algorithm, we develop several new insights into the generalized nested logit model. First, we study nest-specific products that belong to only one nest and show that optimizing over them can be done independently within each nest. Furthermore, within each nest, instead of having to consider all subsets of nest-specific products, it suffices to only consider revenue-ordered subsets (Theorem 4.1). This result allows us to restrict our attention to overlapping products that belong to at least two nests. Second, we establish important structural properties of a tree decomposition of a product graph. Lemma 4.2 shows that for each subtree in the tree decomposition of the product graph, products that share common nests are all located within the subtree, enabling us to use nodes in the tree decomposition as state variables in our dynamic programming algorithm. Lemma 4.3 further shows that the nests of the products associated with a subtree at a particular node can be partitioned as a disjoint union of nests associated with each child node. This partition of nests allows us to efficiently design a polynomial-time dynamic programming algorithm to compute an optimal assortment (Theorem 4.4). To our knowledge, this is the first polynomial-time algorithm for assortment optimization under the generalized nested logit model.

A fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for nest graphs with bounded treewidths:

Section 5 considers the case where the treewidth of the product graph is unbounded, but the nest graph has a bounded treewidth. Theorem 5.3 shows that we can still obtain a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) in this case. Our algorithm exploits special properties of the tree decomposition of the nest graph. Analogous to the properties of the tree decomposition of the product graph, we establish structural properties of the tree decomposition of the nest graph. Lemma 5.1 shows that for each subtree in the tree decomposition of the nest graph, nests that share common products are all located within the subtree. Lemma 5.2 shows that products belonging to nests associated with a subtree at a particular node can be partitioned as a disjoint union of products associated with each child node. In Theorem 5.6, we combine these structural insights with methods for solving multidimensional knapsack problems to design a dynamic programming method that yields an FPTAS. The treewidths of product graph and nest graph can be very different, and thus, both the exact algorithm in Section 4 and the FPTAS in Section 5 are useful. Existing methods in the literature give an FPTAS whose running time is exponential in the number of nests. Our proposed method, however, has a running time that is exponential in the treewidth of the nest graph. The treewidth of the nest graph is always bounded above by the number of nests, but the treewidth can be substantially smaller in many problem instances. Obtaining an FPTAS whose running time scales with the treewidth is the first result of its kind for this choice model.

Empirical results:

Using real transaction data from retailers, we compare the predictive accuracy of the generalized nested logit model with that of the multinomial logit, nested logit, and mixture of multinomial logit models. Across a wide range of product categories, we find that the generalized nested logit model predicts customer purchases more accurately. We also observe similar results on synthetic datasets. This result shows that the generalized nested logit model captures the substitution patterns in retail transactions better than the benchmarks we consider.

1.1 Literature Review

Belonging to the family of generalized extreme value models (McFadden 1978), the generalized nested logit model includes the nested logit models as special cases. The nested logit corresponds to the case in which the nests are nonoverlapping. Some researchers use the name cross-nested logit model (Bierlaire 2006) to refer to the generalized nested logit model. We adopt the terminology of the generalized nested logit model, which was also used by Wen and Koppelman (2001), to emphasize that the model is a generalization of the nested logit model.

The generalized nested logit model includes other choice models as special cases, including the paired combinatorial logit model in which each nest consists of a pair of products (Chu 1989, Koppelman and Wen 2000), the ordered GEV model in which there is a linear ordering on the set of products and each nest consists of a contiguous set of products (Small 1987), and the product differentiation model in which each product is described by a vector of pre-selected features and is assigned to a nest based on the features (Bresnahan et al. 1997).

By allowing for overlapping nests, the product utilities under the generalized nested logit model can exhibit complex correlation patterns, and there is a lot of research on understanding these patterns; see, for example, Abbe et al. (2007), Marzano and Papola (2008), Marzano et al. (2013). Researchers have applied the generalized nested logit model to uncover complex substitution patterns in people migration (Beine et al. 2025), air carrier choices (Drabas and Wu 2013), travel mode and departure time choices in Maryland-Washington D.C. region (Ding et al. 2015), residential location choices (Yang et al. 2013), and many others.

Yet, there has been very limited work on solving operational problems under the generalized nested logit model. Le and Mai (2024) are the first to consider the problem of constrained assortment optimization under the generalized nested logit model with partially captured nests, in which the outside option may appear in every nest. After showing that the unconstrained assortment optimization problem is NP-hard, they develop a discretization heuristic and solve the approximate problem as a mixed-integer linear program. Zhang et al. (2025) consider the cardinality-constrained version, develop a branch-and-bound method to solve the problem exactly, and design heuristics that yield near-optimal solutions in numerical experiments. Pham and Mai (2025) consider the joint assortment and pricing problem, reformulate the problem into bilinear and exponential-cone convex programs, and develop a heuristic to generate strong cutting planes within the branch-and-cut framework. None of these methods is a polynomial-time algorithm in the worst case, and none offers theoretical performance guarantees.

In contrast, we consider the generalized nested logit model with fully captured nests, in which the outside option appears only in its own dedicated nest, and prove that the assortment optimization is NP-hard. We are the first to introduce novel concepts of product and nest graphs, along with their tree decompositions. We show that if the treewidth of the product graph is bounded, then the corresponding assortment optimization problem can be solved in polynomial time. If the treewidth of the product graph is unbounded, but the treewidth of the nest graph remains bounded, then the assortment optimization problem admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. To our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-time algorithms with provable performance guarantees for assortment optimization problems under the generalized nested logit model.

We note that using the approach in the seminal work of Désir et al. (2022), who consider a more general optimization problem, we can obtain an FPTAS for the assortment optimization problem under the generalized nested logit model, with a running time that increases exponentially with the number of nests. In contrast, our FPTAS has a running time that scales more gracefully with the treewidth of the nest graph. Our work is also related to the large literature on assortment optimization under the multinomial logit (Talluri and van Ryzin 2004, Sumida et al. 2021), the nested logit (Davis et al. 2014, Feldman and Topaloglu 2015), and the mixture of multinomial logit (Mendez-Diaz et al. 2010, Désir et al. 2020), and many others; see Ma (2024) for an overview.

The treewidth is one of the most fundamental concepts in graph theory and graph algorithms. The concept was introduced and rediscovered multiple times; see, for example, Halin (1976), Robertson and Seymour (1984), Robertson and Seymour (1986). It is well known that many NP-hard optimization problems on graphs can be solved in polynomial-time when the treewidth of the input graph is bounded; see, for example, Bodlaender (1988), Courcelle (1990), Courcelle (1992). To our knowledge, however, this is the first paper that establishes connections between the complexity of the assortment optimization problem and the treewidths of the product and nest graphs. We believe the concept of treewidth and tree decomposition, on appropriately constructed graphs, can be applied to other problems.

1.2 Organization

Section 2 describes the assortment optimization problem and establishes its computational complexity. Section 3 introduces the product and nest graphs, establishes properties associated with their tree decompositions, and outlines the solution framework. Section 4 describes a fully polynomial-time algorithm for the case where the product graph has a bounded treewidth. Section 5 describes an FPTAS for the case where the nest graph has bounded treewidth. Section 6 contains numerical experiments on real datasets and Section 7 concludes with directions for future research.

2 Assortment Optimization under the Generalized Nested Logit Model

Following the formulation in Wen and Koppelman (2001) and Abbe et al. (2007), the generalized nested logit model is defined as follows. We have a universe of nn products indexed by N={1,2,…,n}N=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}, and the outside option is denoted by product 00, corresponding to the no-purchase option. Under the generalized nested logit model, there is a collection of possibly overlapping subsets of products indexed by K={1,2,…,m}K=\{1,2,\dots,m\}; we refer to these subsets as nests. For each nest k∈Kk\in K, let Mk⊆NM_{k}\subseteq N denote the set of products belonging to nest kk. Each product i∈Ni\in N can belong to multiple nests. The outside option belongs to its own nest, which consists only of product 00.

Letting UiU_{i} denote the utility of product i∈N∪{0}i\in N\cup\{0\}, we assume that Ui=log⁡wi+ϵiU_{i}=\log w_{i}+\epsilon_{i}, where wi>0w_{i}>0 denotes the product-specific constants, with w0=1w_{0}=1. The generating function GG is given by: G⁡(y0,y1,…,yn)=y0+∑k∈K(∑i∈Mk(αi​k​yi)1/γk)γkG(y_{0},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})=y_{0}+\sum_{k\in K}\Big(\sum_{i\in M_{k}}\big(\alpha_{ik}y_{i}\big)^{1/\gamma_{k}}\Big)^{\gamma_{k}}. For each nest k∈Kk\in K, γk∈(0,1]\gamma_{k}\in(0,1] denotes the nest-specific parameter, and αi​k∈ℝ+\alpha_{ik}\in\mathbb{R}_{+} captures the degree of membership of product ii in nest kk. By definition, αi​k=0\alpha_{ik}=0 for all i∉Mki\notin M_{k}, and ∑k∈Kαi​k=1\sum_{k\in K}\alpha_{ik}=1.

The utility specification above shows that the generalized nested logit model is an instance of the Generalized Extreme Value model (McFadden 1978). If we offer an assortment S⊆NS\subseteq N, the probability ϕi​(S)\phi_{i}(S) that a customer will choose product i∈S∪{0}i\in S\cup\{0\} is given by:

Letting Π⁡(S)\Pi(S) denote the expected revenue from offering assortment SS, we have that

We want to find an assortment that maximizes the expected revenue obtained from a customer, corresponding to the following optimization problem:

Z∗=maxS⊆N⁡Π⁡(S).\displaystyle Z^{*}~=~\max_{S\subseteq N}~\Pi(S). (GNL-Assort)

We note that the nested logit model is a special case of the generalized nested logit model in which the nests are assumed to be disjoint; that is, Mk∩Mk′=∅M_{k}\cap M_{k^{\prime}}=\varnothing for k≠k′k\neq k^{\prime}. Davis et al. (2014) proves that the assortment optimization under the nested logit model with partially captured nests (in which the outside option can appear in every nest) is NP-hard, but the problem can be solved in polynomial time in the setting with fully captured nests (in which the outside option appears only in its own dedicated nest). Le and Mai (2024) prove that the assortment optimization problem under the generalized nested logit model with partially captured nests is also NP-hard. However, the complexity of the problem with fully captured nests remains unknown. The following theorem settles this question by showing that the assortment optimization problem under the generalized nested logit model is NP-hard even for fully captured nests. The proof is in Appendix A.1.

Theorem 2.1 (Two Fully Captured Overlapping Nests)

The GNL-Assort problem is NP-hard when there are two fully captured overlapping nests.

Theorem 2.1 uses an instance in which the two nests share all but one product. Complementing this result, we consider the opposite extreme, where any two nests share at most one product.

Theorem 2.2 (Fully Captured Nests Sharing At Most One Product)

The GNL-Assort problem is NP-hard even when |Mk∩Mk′|≤1|M_{k}\cap M_{k^{\prime}}|\leq 1 for all nests k≠k′k\neq k^{\prime}.

The proof of Theorem 2.2 is in Appendix A.2, uses a reduction from the partition problem, and considers an instance in which the number of nests is half the number of products. We note that Zhang et al. (2020) prove that under the paired combinatorial logit model, the assortment optimization problem is also NP-hard, but they use an instance in which the number of nests is at least the number of products raised to the power of 3/23/2, so the number of nests is much larger than the number of products. Theorem 2.2 shows that the problem remains NP-hard even when any two nests share at most one product, and the number of nests is only half the number of products.

In the next section, we introduce product and nest graphs and show how their treewidths can be used to characterize the complexity of the assortment optimization problem. It will turn out that the instances in Theorems 2.1 and 2.2 admit a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme.

3 Product and Nest Graphs

To capture the degrees of overlap across nests, we introduce product and nest graphs. These graphs represent the overlaps among products and nests from complementary perspectives. The structural properties of these graphs will allow us to identify conditions under which the assortment optimization problem is tractable.

Product Graph: For each k∈Kk\in K, define M^k={i∈Mk:∃k′∈K∖{k}​ such that ​i∈Mk′},{\widehat{M}}_{k}=\{i\in M_{k}:\exists\,k^{\prime}\in K\setminus\{k\}\text{ such that }i\in M_{k^{\prime}}\}, which corresponds to the set of products in MkM_{k} that also appear in at least one other nest; that is, M^k=⋃ℓ≠k(Mℓ∩Mk){\widehat{M}}_{k}=\bigcup_{\ell\neq k}(M_{\ell}\cap M_{k}). Letting N^=⋃k∈KM^k{\widehat{N}}=\bigcup_{k\in K}{\widehat{M}}_{k}, products in N^{\widehat{N}} are referred to as overlapping products because they belong to at least two nests, and products in N∖N^N\setminus{\widehat{N}} are nest-specific products because they belong to only one nest. The product graph is then defined as G𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽=(N^,E𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽)G_{\sf Prod}=({\widehat{N}},E_{\sf Prod}), where an edge {i,j}∈E𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽\{i,j\}\in E_{\sf Prod} exists between i,j∈N^i,j\in{\widehat{N}} if and only if there exists a nest k∈Kk\in K such that i∈M^ki\in{\widehat{M}}_{k} and j∈M^kj\in{\widehat{M}}_{k}. Nest-specific products that belong to exactly one nest never appear in G𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽G_{\sf Prod}. We show later that these products can be handled separately in the assortment optimization problem.

Nest Graph: The second graph, denoted by G𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍=(K,E𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍)G_{\sf Nest}=(K,E_{\sf Nest}), captures how nests overlap with one another. In the nest graph, each vertex corresponds to a nest k∈Kk\in K, and an edge {k,ℓ}∈E𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍\{k,\ell\}\in E_{\sf Nest} exists if and only if Mk∩Mℓ≠∅M_{k}\cap M_{\ell}\neq~\varnothing. Thus, two nests are adjacent in G𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍G_{\sf Nest} if they share at least one product. The nest graph therefore encodes the connectivity structure among nests that arises from products that belong to multiple nests.

The following examples illustrate the product and nest graphs. As a convention, we use a circle to represent a vertex in a product graph and a square to represent a vertex in a nest graph.

Example 3.1 (Ordered GEV)

Suppose there are 10 products indexed by {1,2,…,10}\{1,2,\ldots,10\} and eight nests, where each nest is defined as Mi={i,i+1,i+2}M_{i}=\{i,i+1,i+2\} for i∈{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8}i\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8\}. This nest structure is known as the ordered GEV model (Small 1987), which is motivated by settings in which alternatives are naturally ordered, for example by price or quality. In this example, we have N^={2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9}{\widehat{N}}=\{2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9\}. By construction of the ordered GEV model, there exists an edge between products i,j∈N^i,j\in{\widehat{N}} if |i−j|≤2|i-j|\leq 2. The corresponding product and nest graphs are in Figure 1.

Example 3.2 (Economy vs Business Seats in Parallel Flights)

We consider another example based on the product differentiation model (Bresnahan et al. 1997). Consider a direct flight between two locations on a particular day. Suppose the airline offers dd different departure times during the day indexed by t∈{1,2,…,d}t\in\{1,2,\ldots,d\}, and each customer can buy either a business (B) or economy (E) seat. Each product is thus an ordered pair (t,c)(t,c), where t∈{1,…,d}t\in\{1,\ldots,d\} denotes the flight departure time and c∈{B,E}c\in\{B,E\} denotes the seat type, so N={(t,c):t∈{1,…,d},c∈{B,E}}N=\{(t,c):t\in\{1,\ldots,d\},c\in\{B,E\}\}. We construct the nests as follows. Let ME={(t,E):t=1,…,d}M_{E}=\{(t,E)\,:\,t=1,\ldots,d\} be a nest consisting of all the economy-class seats and MB={(t,B):t=1,…,d}M_{B}=\{(t,B)\,:\,t=1,\ldots,d\} a nest consisting of all the business-class seats. For t=1,…,dt=1,\ldots,d, let Mt={(t,B),(t,E)}M_{t}=\{(t,B),(t,E)\} be a nest consisting of flights with a departure time tt. The nests MEM_{E} and MBM_{B} capture substitution among flight options for customers who are indifferent to departure times but care about service levels (either business- or economy-class). In contrast, each nest MtM_{t} represents customers with a specific preference for flights departing at a particular time. Figure 2 shows the product and nest graphs when we have four different departure times (d=4d=4).

The product and nest graphs highlight different but complementary aspects of the generalized nested logit model. The product graph focuses on relationships among products that create non-trivial dependence across nests, while the nest graph summarizes the connectivity pattern among nests induced by products. These graph representations will provide a unified framework for understanding when the assortment optimization problem is computationally tractable.

3.1 Tree Decomposition and Treewidth

To analyze the complexity of the product and nest graphs, we make use of the tree decomposition. We begin by introducing its formal definition.

Definition 3.3 (Tree decomposition)

Given an undirected graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), a tree decomposition of GG is a connected tree 𝖳{{\sf T}} on a new set of nodes 𝖡{\sf B}, where each b∈𝖡b\in{\sf B} corresponds to a subset Vtcs​(b)\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right) of vertices of VV and is referred to as a bag of vertices. The tree decomposition has the following three properties:

  1. 1.

    ⋃b∈𝖡Vtcs​(b)=V\bigcup_{b\in{\sf B}}\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right)=V.

  2. 2.

    For every edge (i,j)∈E(i,j)\in E, there exists b∈𝖡b\in{\sf B} such that {i,j}⊆Vtcs​(b)\{i,j\}\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right).

  3. 3.

    For any a,b,c∈𝖡a,b,c\in{\sf B}, if bb lies on the path in 𝖳{{\sf T}} from aa to cc, then Vtcs​(a)∩Vtcs​(c)⊆Vtcs​(b)\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(a\right)\cap\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(c\right)\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right).

The width of the tree decomposition 𝖳{{\sf T}} is equal to the size of the largest bag (set of vertices) minus one; that is, maxb∈𝖡⁡|Vtcs​(b)|−1\max_{b\in{\sf B}}|\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right)|-1. A trivial tree decomposition is a tree with a single bag consisting of all vertices of the original graph. The treewidth of a graph GG, denoted by 𝗍𝗐⁡(G){\sf tw}(G), is the minimum width among all tree decompositions of GG. Throughout our paper, we also assume without loss of generality that each tree decomposition has at most |V||V| nodes. This follows by removing “redundant” bags; see Kleinberg and Tardos (2006) Section 10.4 for details.

To illustrate a tree decomposition, we reuse the graph structures introduced in the previous section as an illustrative example. The left side of Figure 3 presents a valid tree decomposition of the product graph in Example 3.1, and the right side shows a valid tree decomposition of the nest graph in Example 3.2. The directed edges indicate the orientation of the tree, with node aa corresponding to the root of the tree. Each node in the tree decomposition corresponds to a subset of vertices from the original graph, either a subset of products for the product graph or a subset of nests for the nest graph. In this example, every node in the decomposition contains three vertices, implying that the tree decomposition has width of 22. Under this example, the treewidth is also 22.

To streamline the discussion, we introduce notation to describe the components of a tree decomposition. Given a node b∈𝖡b\in{\sf B}, we write 𝖯𝖺⁡(b){\sf Pa}(b) for the parent of bb in the tree, 𝖢𝗁⁡(b){\sf Ch}(b) for the set of its children, and 𝖣𝖾⁡(b){\sf De}(b) for the set of nodes that can be reached from node bb in the directed tree, the descendants of bb. By convention, we let b∈𝖣𝖾⁡(b)b\in{\sf De}(b). We then define the head of bb as Head​(b)=Vtcs​(b)∩Vtcs​(𝖯𝖺⁡(b))\textit{{Head}}\left(b\right)=\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right)\cap\textit{{Vtcs}}\left({\sf Pa}(b)\right) and Tail​(b)=Vtcs​(b)∖Head​(b)\textit{{Tail}}\left(b\right)=\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right)\setminus\textit{{Head}}\left(b\right). Note that Head​(b)∩Tail​(b)=∅\textit{{Head}}\left(b\right)\cap\textit{{Tail}}\left(b\right)=\varnothing and Vtcs​(b)=Head​(b)∪⋅Tail​(b)\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right)=\textit{{Head}}\left(b\right)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\textit{{Tail}}\left(b\right); we use ∪⋅\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}} to denote disjoint union. Finally, we define Subt​(b)=(⋃a∈𝖣𝖾⁡(b)Vtcs​(a))∖Head​(b)\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right)=\big(\;\bigcup_{a\in{\sf De}(b)}\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(a\right)\;\big)\setminus\textit{{Head}}\left(b\right), which collects all vertices appearing in bags of bb and its descendants, excluding those belonging to Head​(b)\textit{{Head}}\left(b\right). We refer to this as the subtree under node bb. We let 𝗋𝗈𝗈𝗍{\sf root} denote the root node of the tree and, by convention, we set Head​(𝗋𝗈𝗈𝗍)=∅\textit{{Head}}\left({\sf root}\right)=\varnothing. To illustrate these definitions, we refer to the tree decompositions shown in Figure 3. Consider node cc of the tree in the left figure. Its parent is node bb, and its child is node dd. Moreover, the set of descendants of cc is {c,d,e,f}\{c,d,e,f\}. In this case, we have Head​(c)={4,5}\textit{{Head}}\left(c\right)=\{4,5\}, Tail​(c)={6}\textit{{Tail}}\left(c\right)=\{6\}, and Subt​(c)={6,7,8,9}\textit{{Subt}}\left(c\right)=\{6,7,8,9\}. For the right tree in Figure 3, we have that Head​(c)={ME,MB}\textit{{Head}}\left(c\right)=\{M_{E},M_{B}\}, Tail​(c)={M3}\textit{{Tail}}\left(c\right)=\{M_{3}\}, and Subt​(c)={M3,M4}\textit{{Subt}}\left(c\right)=\{M_{3},M_{4}\}. We note the difference in fonts: 𝖯𝖺⁡(b){\sf Pa}(b), 𝖢𝗁⁡(b){\sf Ch}(b), and 𝖣𝖾⁡(b){\sf De}(b) refer to nodes in the tree decomposition, while Head​(b)\textit{{Head}}\left(b\right), Vtcs​(b)\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right), Tail​(b)\textit{{Tail}}\left(b\right), and Subt​(b)\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right) refer to collections of vertices in the original product graph or nest graph.

Intuitively, the set Head​(b)\textit{{Head}}\left(b\right) acts as a separator between Subt​(b)\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right) and the vertices outside the subtree V∖Subt​(b)V\setminus\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right). In particular, there cannot exist an edge connecting a product in Subt​(b)\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right) to a product in V∖Subt​(b)∖Head​(b)V\setminus\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right)\setminus\textit{{Head}}\left(b\right), since such an edge would violate Property 2 of a tree decomposition and lead to a contradiction. This separation implies that the analysis of Subt​(b)\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right) can be confined entirely to the subtree rooted at bb and Head​(b)\textit{{Head}}\left(b\right). The next lemma focuses on the set of vertices in Subt​(b)\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right) and shows that Subt​(b)\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right) can be partitioned into disjoint subsets corresponding to the subtrees of its children together with Tail​(b)\textit{{Tail}}\left(b\right). We will apply this lemma to the tree decompositions of the product and nest graphs (Lemmas 4.3 and 5.2) to establish the separations of the nests and products based on the tree decompositions.

Lemma 3.4 (Separation of Vertices)

For b∈𝖡b\in{\sf B}, Subt​(b)=(⋃⋅a∈𝖢𝗁⁡(b)⁡Subt​(a))​⋃⋅⁡Tail​(b)\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right)=\left(\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits_{a\in{\sf Ch}(b)}\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right)\right)\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits\textit{{Tail}}\left(b\right).

Proof: Because Subt​(b)=(Subt​(b)∖Tail​(b))​⋃⋅⁡Tail​(b)\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right)=(\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right)\setminus\textit{{Tail}}\left(b\right))\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits\textit{{Tail}}\left(b\right), it suffices to show that Subt​(b)∖Tail​(b)=⋃⋅a∈𝖢𝗁⁡(b)⁡Subt​(a)\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right)\setminus\textit{{Tail}}\left(b\right)=\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits_{a\in{\sf Ch}(b)}\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right). To see this, we first obtain the following chain of equalities:

Subt​(b)∖Tail​(b)\displaystyle\textit{{Subt}}\left(b\right)\setminus\textit{{Tail}}\left(b\right) =(⋃a∈𝖣𝖾⁡(b)Vtcs​(a)∖Head​(b))∖Tail​(b)​=(i)​(⋃a∈𝖣𝖾⁡(b)∖{b}Vtcs​(a))∖Vtcs​(b)\displaystyle~=~\bigg(\bigcup_{a\in{\sf De}(b)}\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(a\right)\setminus\textit{{Head}}\left(b\right)\bigg)\setminus\textit{{Tail}}\left(b\right)\overset{(i)}{=}\bigg(\bigcup_{a\in{\sf De}(b)\setminus\{b\}}\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(a\right)\bigg)\setminus\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right)
=(i​i)​(⋃a∈𝖢𝗁⁡(b)(Subt​(a)∪Head​(a)))∖Vtcs​(b)​=(i​i​i)​⋃a∈𝖢𝗁⁡(b)Subt​(a),\displaystyle~\overset{(ii)}{=}~\bigg(\bigcup_{a\in{\sf Ch}(b)}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\Big(\;\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right)\cup\textit{{Head}}\left(a\right)\;\Big)}}\bigg)\setminus\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right)\overset{(iii)}{=}\bigcup_{a\in{\sf Ch}(b)}\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right),

where (i)(i) follows from Head​(b)∪⋅Tail​(b)=Vtcs​(b)\textit{{Head}}\left(b\right)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\textit{{Tail}}\left(b\right)=\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right), and (i​i)(ii) follows from the definition of subtree. The last equality (i​i​i)(iii) follows because Subt​(a)∩Vtcs​(b)=∅\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right)\cap\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right)=\varnothing for a∈𝖢𝗁⁡(b)a\in{\sf Ch}(b). This holds because a path from a descendant of aa to bb must go through the node aa. By Property 3 of the tree decomposition, if k∈Subt​(a)∩Vtcs​(b)k\in\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right)\cap\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right), then we must have k∈Vtcs​(a)k\in\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(a\right). Because b=𝖯𝖺⁡(a)b={\sf Pa}(a), it follows that k∈Vtcs​(a)∩Vtcs​(𝖯𝖺⁡(a))=Head​(a)k\in\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(a\right)\cap\textit{{Vtcs}}\left({\sf Pa}(a)\right)=\textit{{Head}}\left(a\right), which raises a contradiction since Head​(a)\textit{{Head}}\left(a\right) and Subt​(a)\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right) are disjoint. Also, notice that Head​(a)⊆Vtcs​(b)\textit{{Head}}\left(a\right)\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right) so we have (Subt​(a)∪Head​(a))∖Vtcs​(b)=Subt​(a)(\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right)\cup\textit{{Head}}\left(a\right))\setminus\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right)=\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right).

To complete the proof, it suffices to show that for a,a′∈𝖢𝗁⁡(b)a,a^{\prime}\in{\sf Ch}(b) with a≠a′a\neq a^{\prime} , we have Subt​(a)∩Subt​(a′)=∅\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right)\cap\textit{{Subt}}\left(a^{\prime}\right)=\varnothing. We prove a stronger claim here, where we show Subt​(a)∩(Subt​(a′)∪Head​(a′))=∅\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right)\cap(\textit{{Subt}}\left(a^{\prime}\right)\cup\textit{{Head}}\left(a^{\prime}\right))=\varnothing for a,a′∈𝖢𝗁⁡(b)a,a^{\prime}\in{\sf Ch}(b) with a≠a′a\neq a^{\prime} . By contradiction, we assume that Subt​(a)∩(Subt​(a′)∪Head​(a′))≠∅\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right)\cap(\textit{{Subt}}\left(a^{\prime}\right)\cup\textit{{Head}}\left(a^{\prime}\right))\neq\varnothing so there exists a vertex kk such that k∈Subt​(a)k\in\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right) and k∈Subt​(a′)∪Head​(a′)k\in\textit{{Subt}}\left(a^{\prime}\right)\cup\textit{{Head}}\left(a^{\prime}\right). This indicates that there must exist a node in 𝖣𝖾⁡(a){\sf De}(a) that contains kk and similarly, there must also exist a node in 𝖣𝖾⁡(a′){\sf De}(a^{\prime}) that contains kk as well. Recall that both node aa and a′a^{\prime} are the children of bb so any path from a node in 𝖣𝖾⁡(a){\sf De}(a) to another node in 𝖣𝖾⁡(a′){\sf De}(a^{\prime}) must pass through aa, a′a^{\prime} and bb. By Property 3 of the tree decomposition, this indicates k∈Vtcs​(a)k\in\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(a\right) and k∈Vtcs​(b)k\in\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(b\right). Because b=𝖯𝖺⁡(a)b={\sf Pa}(a), we have k∈Head​(a)k\in\textit{{Head}}\left(a\right), but this is impossible because Head​(a)∩Subt​(a)=∅\textit{{Head}}\left(a\right)\cap\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right)=\varnothing! Therefore, it must be the case that Subt​(a)∩Subt​(a′)=∅\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right)\cap\textit{{Subt}}\left(a^{\prime}\right)=\varnothing.  

To close this section, we summarize two existing algorithms for constructing tree decompositions. When the treewidth of a graph is bounded by a constant, Bodlaender (1996) provides a linear-time algorithm that constructs a tree decomposition with the treewidth. For general graphs, Feige et al. (2005) develop a polynomial-time algorithm that constructs a tree decomposition of width O⁡(w​log⁡w)O(w\sqrt{\log w}), where ww is the treewidth of the graph.

3.2 Solution Framework

Following the approach of Davis et al. (2014) and Zhang et al. (2020), we reformulate the GNL-Assort problem into an equivalent formulation that involves finding a fixed point of a nonincreasing function. To see this, note that for each S⊆NS\subseteq N, Π⁡(S)=∑k∈KVk​(S)γk​Rk​(S)1+∑ℓ∈KVℓ​(S)γℓ≥z\Pi(S)=\sum_{k\in K}\frac{V_{k}(S)^{\gamma_{k}}R_{k}(S)}{1+\sum_{\ell\in K}V_{\ell}(S)^{\gamma_{\ell}}}\geq z if and only if ∑k∈KVk​(S)γk​(Rk​(S)−z)≥z.\sum_{k\in K}V_{k}(S)^{\gamma_{k}}\big(R_{k}(S)-z\big)\geq z. We define the function F:ℝ+→ℝ+F:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} as follows: for each z∈ℝ+z\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, F⁡(z)=maxS⊆N⁡{∑k∈KVk​(S)γk​(Rk​(S)−z)}.F(z)\;=\;\max_{S\subseteq N}\left\{\sum_{k\in K}V_{k}(S)^{\gamma_{k}}\big(R_{k}(S)-z\big)\right\}. The following lemma establishes the connection between this function and the optimal value Z∗Z^{*} of the GNL-Assort problem.

Lemma 3.5

The optimal value Z∗Z^{*} of the GNL-Assort problem is the unique fixed point of the function FF; that is, F⁡(Z∗)=Z∗F(Z^{*})=Z^{*}. Moreover, if S∗=\argmaxS⊆N​{∑k∈KVk​(S)γk​(Rk​(S)−Z∗)}S^{*}=\argmax_{S\subseteq N}\left\{\sum_{k\in K}V_{k}(S)^{\gamma_{k}}\big(R_{k}(S)-Z^{*}\big)\right\}, then S∗S^{*} is an optimal solution to the GNL-Assort problem.

The proof of Lemma 3.5 follows the same argument as in Gallego and Topaloglu (2014) and is therefore omitted. Consider the equation z=F⁡(z)z=F(z). Since the left-hand side is strictly increasing in zz, while F⁡(z)F(z) is continuous and nonincreasing, the equation z=F⁡(z)z=F(z) admits a unique solution. This solution can be computed via a standard binary search over an interval that contains the optimal objective value. At each iteration of the binary search, we evaluate F⁡(z)F(z) at the midpoint of the current interval and update the interval depending on whether F⁡(z)F(z) lies above or below zz. Such procedures are standard in the revenue management literature; see, for example, Alfandari et al. (2021). The above argument implies that if F⁡(z)F(z) can be evaluated exactly in polynomial time, then the optimal objective value z^\hat{z} can be computed within an additive error ϵ\epsilon, with a running time that is polynomial in the input size and log⁡(1/ϵ)\log(1/\epsilon). Moreover, if F⁡(z)F(z) cannot be evaluated exactly but admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme, then a similar procedure yields a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for the GNL-Assort problem. For completeness, we state and prove this result in Appendix B.1.

Theorem 3.6 (Using F⁡(z)F(z) to Solve GNL-Assort Problem)

If we can compute F⁡(z)F(z) exactly in polynomial time for every z∈ℝ+z\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, then we can solve the GNL-Assort problem within an additive error ϵ\epsilon, with a running time that is polynomial in the input size and log⁡(1/ϵ)\log(1/\epsilon). If there is a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme to approximate F⁡(z)F(z) for every z∈ℝ+z\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, then we also have a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for the GNL-Assort problem with a multiplicative error ϵ\epsilon, with a running time that is polynomial in the input size and 1/ϵ1/\epsilon.

By Theorem 3.6, in the remainder of this manuscript, we focus on developing efficient methods for approximately evaluating F⁡(z)F(z) at a fixed value of zz. Note that the objective function of F⁡(z)F(z) can be written as ∑k∈KVk​(S)γk​(Rk​(S)−z)=∑k∈K∑i∈Svi​k​(fi−z)Vk​(S)1−γk\sum_{k\in K}V_{k}(S)^{\gamma_{k}}\big(R_{k}(S)-z\big)=\sum_{k\in K}\frac{\sum_{i\in S}v_{ik}(f_{i}-z)}{V_{k}(S)^{1-\gamma_{k}}}. To streamline our discussion, we let ri=fi−zr_{i}=f_{i}-z and we focus on solving the following optimization problem

F∗=max⁡∑k∈KS⊆N⁡∑i∈Svi​k​riVk​(S)1−γk.F^{*}=\max_{S\subseteq N}~\sum_{k\in K}\frac{\sum_{i\in S}v_{ik}r_{i}}{V_{k}(S)^{1-\gamma_{k}}}. (Aux-Assort)

In the Aux-Assort problem above, the revenue rir_{i} may be negative. However, it is without loss of generality to assume ri≥0r_{i}\geq 0 for all i∈Ni\in N. To see this, for each S⊆NS\subseteq N, let ηi​(S)=∑k∈Kvi​k/(Vk​(S))1−γk\eta_{i}(S)=\sum_{k\in K}v_{ik}/\big(V_{k}(S)\big)^{1-\gamma_{k}}, and it follows that F∗=max⁡∑i∈SS⊆N⁡ri​ηi​(S)F^{*}=\max_{S\subseteq N}\sum_{i\in S}r_{i}\eta_{i}(S). For any assortment SS, let BS={i∈S:ri<0}B_{S}=\{i\in S\,:\,r_{i}<0\} denote all the products in SS with negative revenue. Then, we have that ∑i∈S∖Bri​ηi​(S∖B)≥∑i∈Sri​ηi​(S)\sum_{i\in S\setminus B}r_{i}\eta_{i}(S\setminus B)\geq\sum_{i\in S}r_{i}\eta_{i}(S) because γk∈(0,1]\gamma_{k}\in(0,1] for all kk, so for each i∈S∖Bi\in S\setminus B, ηi​(S∖B)≥ηi​(S)\eta_{i}(S\setminus B)\geq\eta_{i}(S) by definition. Thus, any assortment SS containing products with negative revenue can be improved by removing those products. We can therefore restrict attention to the case ri≥0r_{i}\geq 0 for all i∈Ni\in N. Our goal in the following sections is to develop an efficient way of computing or approximating F∗F^{*}. To close this section, the following theorem shows that it is NP-hard to approximate the Aux-Assort problem within any constant factor.

Theorem 3.7 (Hardness of the Aux-Assort Problem)

Letting m=|K|m=|K|, the Aux-Assort problem is NP-hard to approximate within O⁡(1/m1−δ)O(1/m^{1-\delta}) for any δ>0\delta>0.

The proof is deferred to Appendix B.2. It is based on a reduction from the maximum independent set problem, which is known to be NP-hard to approximate within any constant factor. We highlight two important remarks. First, the proof applies specifically to the Aux-Assort problem and does not directly imply that the overall assortment optimization problem under the generalized nested logit model inherits the same hardness of approximation. In fact, whether the GNL-Assort problem itself is NP-hard to approximate within O⁡(1/m1−δ)O(1/m^{1-\delta}) for any δ>0\delta>0 remains, to the best of our knowledge, an open question. Second, although the reduction shows that the Aux-Assort problem is NP-hard to approximate within any constant factor, the construction relies on instances with a highly intricate structure of the nests. As a result, this does not rule out the possibility that the Aux-Assort problem, and consequently the assortment optimization problem, may be tractable in settings with more structured nest configurations. We characterize such cases in the following sections.

4 A Polynomial-time Algorithm for Product Graphs with Bounded Treewidths

Letting the tree decomposition over the product graph be denoted by 𝖳𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽=(𝖡𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽,𝖤𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽){{\sf T}}_{\sf Prod}=({\sf B}_{\sf Prod},{\sf E}_{\sf Prod}), we will use 𝖳𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽{{\sf T}}_{\sf Prod} to develop an algorithm for the Aux-Assort problem. In this section, for any p∈𝖡𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽p\in{\sf B}_{\sf Prod}, the set Vtcs​(p)\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right), Head​(p)\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right), Subt​(p)\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right) and Tail​(p)\textit{{Tail}}\left(p\right) correspond to sets of products. We first give a few important structural properties of the tree decomposition over the product graph and then discuss a dynamic program to solve the Aux-Assort problem.

4.1 Properties of Nest-Specific Products

Recall from the previous section that the vertices of the product graph G𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽G_{\sf Prod} consist of overlapping products that belong to at least two nests, corresponding to N^{\widehat{N}}. To analyze our algorithm, we first isolate the products specific to a single nest, corresponding to N∖N^N\setminus{\widehat{N}}, which we refer to as the nest-specific products. For these products, we establish that the optimal assortment exhibits a revenue-ordered structure. To see this, we first rewrite the Aux-Assort problem as follows:

F∗=maxS⊆N⁡{∑k∈K∑i∈Svi​k​riVk​(S)1−γk}​=(i)​maxS^⊆N^​{∑k∈KmaxTk⊆Mk∖M^k⁡∑i∈S^∪⋅Tkvi​k​riVk​(S^∪⋅Tk)1−γk},F^{*}~=~\max_{S\subseteq N}\left\{\sum_{k\in K}\frac{\sum_{i\in S}v_{ik}r_{i}}{V_{k}(S)^{1-\gamma_{k}}}\right\}~\overset{(i)}{=}\max_{{\widehat{S}}\subseteq{\widehat{N}}}~\left\{~\sum_{k\in K}~\max_{T_{k}\subseteq M_{k}\setminus{\widehat{M}}_{k}}~\frac{\sum_{i\in{\widehat{S}}\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}T_{k}}v_{ik}r_{i}}{V_{k}({\widehat{S}}\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}T_{k})^{1-\gamma_{k}}}~\right\},

where (i)(i) follows from the fact that Mk∖M^kM_{k}\setminus{\widehat{M}}_{k} consists of nest-specific products that only belong to nest kk. Once we fix S^⊆N^{\widehat{S}}\subseteq{\widehat{N}}, the optimization over the remaining nest-specific products can be carried out independently within each nest. The following theorem shows that once S^{\widehat{S}} is fixed, an optimal subset of nest-specific products is revenue-ordered.

For each S^⊆N^{\widehat{S}}\subseteq{\widehat{N}} and k∈Kk\in K, there exists a revenue-ordered subset that is an optimal solution to the optimization problem maxTk⊆Mk∖M^k⁡(∑i∈S^∪⋅Tkvi​k​ri)/Vk​(S^∪⋅Tk)1−γk\max_{T_{k}\subseteq M_{k}\setminus{\widehat{M}}_{k}}~\big(\sum_{i\in{\widehat{S}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}}}T_{k}}v_{ik}r_{i}\big)/V_{k}({\widehat{S}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}}}T_{k})^{1-\gamma_{k}}; that is, there exists an optimal solution Tk∗​(S^)T_{k}^{*}({\widehat{S}}) and τk∈ℝ\tau_{k}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\mathbb{R}}} such that Tk∗​(S^)={i∈Mk∖M^k:ri≥τk}T_{k}^{*}({\widehat{S}})=\{i\in M_{k}\setminus{\widehat{M}}_{k}\,:\,r_{i}\geq\tau_{k}\}.

Proof: Fix an arbitrary S^⊆N^{\widehat{S}}\subseteq{\widehat{N}} and k∈Kk\in K. The result follows from Lemma C.5 by Balseiro and Désir (2023), who considered the optimization problem maxS⊆𝒮⁡W⁡(∑i∈Sai,∑i∈Sbi)\max_{S\subseteq{\cal S}}W(\sum_{i\in S}a_{i}\,,\,\sum_{i\in S}b_{i}), where 𝒮{\cal S} denotes the collection of subsets, the vectors 𝒂,𝒃\bm{a},\bm{b} are nonnegative, and W:ℝ2→ℝW:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} is a quasiconvex function. Because the function WW is increasing in xx and decreasing in yy, it follows that λ>0\lambda>0. We note an immediate implication for the GNL-Assort problem. 4.2 Properties of Tree Decomposition over Product Graph

We discuss two important properties of a tree decomposition over the product graph. For each i∈Ni\in N, let 𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(i)={k∈K:i∈Mk}{\sf Nest}(i)=\{k\in K\,:\,i\in M_{k}\} denote the set of nests that contain product ii, and 𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(S)=⋃i∈S𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(i){\sf Nest}(S)=\bigcup_{i\in S}{\sf Nest}(i) denote the set of nests associated with products in SS. For each p∈𝖡𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽p\in{\sf B}_{\sf Prod}, the next lemma shows that all products belonging to the same nests as products in Subt​(p)\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right) must be contained in Subt​(p)∪⋅Head​(p)\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right); that is, ∪k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍​(Subt​(p))M^k⊆Subt(p)∪⋅Head(p)\cup_{k\in{\sf Nest}(\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right))}{\widehat{M}}_{k}\subseteq\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right). This lemma ensures that computations involving products at node pp can be performed without having to consider products outside the subtree.

Lemma 4.2 (Subtree Contains All Related Products)

For p∈𝖡𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽p\in{\sf B}_{\sf Prod} and k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍​(Subt​(p))k\in{\sf Nest}(\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)), M^k⊆Subt​(p)∪⋅Head​(p){\widehat{M}}_{k}\subseteq\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right).

Proof: The claim is trivial when p=𝗋𝗈𝗈𝗍p={\sf root} because Subt​(𝗋𝗈𝗈𝗍)=N^\textit{{Subt}}\left({\sf root}\right)={\widehat{N}}, so assume that p≠𝗋𝗈𝗈𝗍p\neq{\sf root}. Suppose, on the contrary, that there exists a nest k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍​(Subt​(p))k\in{\sf Nest}\big(\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\big) and a product i∈M^ki\in{\widehat{M}}_{k} such that i∉Subt​(p)∪Head​(p)i\notin\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\cup\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right). Because k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍​(Subt​(p))k\in{\sf Nest}\big(\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\big), there exists a product j∈Subt​(p)j\in\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right) such that j∈M^kj\in{\widehat{M}}_{k}. Let a∈𝖣𝖾⁡(p)a\in{\sf De}(p) be such that j∈Vtcs​(a)j\in\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(a\right).

By definition of the product graph G𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽G_{\sf Prod}, (i,j)∈E𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽(i,j)\in E_{\sf Prod} and by Property 2 of the tree decomposition, there exists a bag c∈𝖡𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽c\in{\sf B}_{\sf Prod} such that {i,j}⊆Vtcs​(c)\{i,j\}\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(c\right). Because i∉Subt​(p)∪⋅Head​(p)i\notin\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right), we must have c∉𝖣𝖾⁡(p)c\notin{\sf De}(p). Therefore, node cc must not lie in the subtree under node pp. We consider the path from cc to aa. Because node cc does not lie in the subtree under pp and node aa lies in the subtree under pp, both pp and 𝖯𝖺⁡(p){\sf Pa}(p) are included in the path. By Property 3 of the tree decomposition, we must have Vtcs​(a)∩Vtcs​(c)⊆Vtcs​(𝖯𝖺⁡(p))\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(a\right)\cap\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(c\right)\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left({\sf Pa}(p)\right) and Vtcs​(a)∩Vtcs​(c)⊆Vtcs​(p)\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(a\right)\cap\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(c\right)\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right). Because j∈Vtcs​(a)∩Vtcs​(c)j\in\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(a\right)\cap\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(c\right), we have j∈Vtcs​(𝖯𝖺​(p))j\in\textit{{Vtcs}}\left({\sf Pa}(p)\right) and j∈Vtcs​(p)j\in\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right), which implies that j∈Head​(p)j\in\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right). But we also have j∈Subt​(p)j\in\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right). This is a contradiction because Subt​(p)∩Head​(p)=∅\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\cap\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right)=\varnothing! Thus, we must have M^k⊆Subt​(p)∪⋅Head​(p){\widehat{M}}_{k}\subseteq\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right).  

Recall that Lemma 3.4 establishes a useful separation of the vertices based on the tree decomposition. Since we are working with the tree decomposition over the product graph, this result implies a separation of the products. In the next lemma, we show that a similar separation property holds for the nests as well. The separation of nests across the children of node pp shown in this lemma allows us to perform computation at each child node separately and combine the results together, forming the basis for our dynamic programming method.

Lemma 4.3 (Nest Separation in Product Graph)

For each p∈𝖡𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽p\in{\sf B}_{\sf Prod},

𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(Subt​(p))={k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(Tail​(p)):M^k⊆Vtcs​(p)}​⋃⋅⁡(⋃⋅a∈𝖢𝗁⁡(p)⁡𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(Subt​(a))).{\sf Nest}(\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right))=\big\{k\in{\sf Nest}(\textit{{Tail}}\left(p\right)):{\widehat{M}}_{k}\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right)\big\}\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits\Big(\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits_{a\in{\sf Ch}(p)}{\sf Nest}(\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right))\Big).

Proof: Consider an arbitrary p∈𝖡𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽p\in{\sf B}_{\sf Prod}. Let 𝒟p=Subt​(p)∖Vtcs​(p)=Subt​(p)∖Tail​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{p}=\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\setminus\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right)=\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\setminus\textit{{Tail}}\left(p\right), where the second equality follows because Vtcs​(p)=Head​(p)∪⋅Tail​(p)\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right)=\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\textit{{Tail}}\left(p\right) and Subt​(p)∩Head​(p)=∅\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\cap\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right)=\varnothing. Claim 1: 𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(Subt​(p))∖𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(𝒟p)={k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(Tail​(p)):M^k⊆Vtcs​(p)}{\sf Nest}(\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right))\setminus{\sf Nest}({\mathcal{D}}_{p})=\big\{k\in{\sf Nest}(\textit{{Tail}}\left(p\right)):{\widehat{M}}_{k}\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right)\big\}.

To prove Claim 1, let Kp={k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(Tail​(p)):M^k⊆Vtcs​(p)}K_{p}=\big\{k\in{\sf Nest}(\textit{{Tail}}\left(p\right)):{\widehat{M}}_{k}\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right)\big\}. We will first show Kp⊆𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(Subt​(p))∖𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(𝒟p)K_{p}\subseteq{\sf Nest}\big(\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\big)\setminus{\sf Nest}\big({\mathcal{D}}_{p}\big). Consider an arbitrary k∈Kpk\in K_{p}. By definition, k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍​(Tail​(p))k\in{\sf Nest}(\textit{{Tail}}\left(p\right)) and M^k⊆Vtcs​(p){\widehat{M}}_{k}\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right). Then, k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍​(Subt​(p))k\in{\sf Nest}\big(\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\big) because Tail​(p)⊆Subt​(p)\textit{{Tail}}\left(p\right)\subseteq\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right), and k∉𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(𝒟p)k\notin{\sf Nest}\big({\mathcal{D}}_{p}\big) because M^k⊆Vtcs​(p){\widehat{M}}_{k}\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right), so k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(Subt​(p))∖𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(𝒟p)k\in{\sf Nest}\big(\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right)\big)\setminus{\sf Nest}\big({\mathcal{D}}_{p}\big). Lemmas 4.2 and 4.3 establish a strong separation property of the product graph under tree decomposition. Lemma 4.2 ensures that whenever a nest is associated with products in Subt​(p)\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right), all of its overlapping products are fully contained in the subtree rooted at pp. Building on this, Lemma 4.3 shows how the nests associated with Subt​(p)\textit{{Subt}}\left(p\right) can be partitioned into disjoint components determined by Vtcs​(p)\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right) and the subtrees of its children. This decomposition highlights how both products and nests can be localized within subtrees, which is the key insight that allows us to design a dynamic programming algorithm when the product graph has a bounded treewidth.

4.3 A Dynamic Program to Solve the Aux-Assort Problem

We present a dynamic program to solve the Aux-Assort problem by exploiting the property of nest-specific products in Theorem 4.1 and the structure of the product graph through its tree decomposition as discussed in Lemmas 4.2 and 4.3. Without loss of generality, we assume that the tree decomposition results in a single tree. If the decomposition yields a forest, we can process each tree independently and combine its value. We can also assume that 𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(N^)=K{\sf Nest}({\widehat{N}})=K; that is, every nest contains at least one product that belongs to multiple nests. Hp(S,T)=∑k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(Tail​(p)):M^k⊆Vtcs​(p)maxAk∈𝒪kψk(S∪⋅T∪⋅Ak).H_{p}(S,T)=\sum_{k\in{\sf Nest}(\textit{{Tail}}\left(p\right))\,:\,{\widehat{M}}_{k}\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right)}~~\max_{A_{k}\in{\mathcal{O}}_{k}}\psi_{k}(S\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}T\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}A_{k}).

For each (S,T)∈2Head​(p)×2Tail​(p)(S,T)\in 2^{\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right)}\times 2^{\textit{{Tail}}\left(p\right)}, computing the function Hp​(S,T)H_{p}(S,T) takes O⁡(m​n)O(mn) operations because for each nest kk, computing maxAk∈𝒪k⁡ψk​(S∪⋅T∪⋅Ak)\max_{A_{k}\in{\mathcal{O}}_{k}}\psi_{k}(S\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}T\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}A_{k}) takes O⁡(n)O(n) operations as there are O⁡(n)O(n) revenue-ordered subsets in 𝒪k{\mathcal{O}}_{k}. To see this, recall that ψk​(X)=(∑i∈Xvi​k​ri)/(∑i∈Xvi​k)1−γk\psi_{k}(X)=(\sum_{i\in X}v_{ik}r_{i})/(\sum_{i\in X}v_{ik})^{1-\gamma_{k}} for all XX. To evaluate ψk​(S∪⋅T∪⋅Ak)\psi_{k}(S\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}T\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}A_{k}) for every Ak∈𝒪kA_{k}\in{\mathcal{O}}_{k}, we maintain the sums in the numerator and denominator, and because the sets in 𝒪k{\mathcal{O}}_{k} are sorted, each one is obtained from the previous one by adding just one element; the sums can be updated in O⁡(1)O(1) operations. Because the number of possible (S,T)∈2Head​(p)×2Tail​(p)(S,T)\in 2^{\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right)}\times 2^{\textit{{Tail}}\left(p\right)} is 2|Vtcs​(p)|≤2𝗍𝗐⁡(G𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽)+12^{|\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(p\right)|}\leq 2^{{\sf tw}(G_{\sf Prod})+1} since 𝗍𝗐⁡(G𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽)=maxa∈𝖡𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽⁡|Vtcs​(a)|−1{\sf tw}(G_{\sf Prod})=\max_{a\in{\sf B}_{\sf Prod}}|\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(a\right)|-1, it follows that computing the function HpH_{p} takes O⁡(m​n​ 2𝗍𝗐⁡(G𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽))O\big(m\,n\,2^{{\sf tw}(G_{\sf Prod})}\big) operations. Because the number of bags in a non-redundant tree decomposition of a product graph is O⁡(n)O(n), computing the function HpH_{p} for every p∈𝖡𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽p\in{\sf B}_{\sf Prod} takes O⁡(m​n2​ 2𝗍𝗐⁡(G𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽))O(m\,n^{2}\,2^{{\sf tw}(G_{\sf Prod})}) operations.

The dynamic programming equation can be written as follows: for each S⊆Head​(p)S\subseteq\textit{{Head}}\left(p\right),

Jp𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽​(S)=maxT⊆Tail​(p)⁡{Hp​(S,T)+∑a∈𝖢𝗁⁡(p)Ja𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽​((S∪⋅T)∩Head​(a))}.J^{\sf Prod}_{p}(S)~=~\max_{T\subseteq\textit{{Tail}}\left(p\right)}\Big\{~H_{p}(S,T)+\sum_{a\in{\sf Ch}(p)}J^{{\sf Prod}}_{a}\big((S\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}T)\cap\textit{{Head}}\left(a\right)\big)~\Big\}~.

Having computed HpH_{p} for all p∈𝖡𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽p\in{\sf B}_{\sf Prod}, we can recursively compute the value functions starting from the leaf nodes. The time it takes to compute the value function Jp𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽J^{\sf Prod}_{p} is O⁡(2𝗍𝗐⁡(G𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽)​(1+|𝖢𝗁⁡(p)|))O\Big(2^{{\sf tw}(G_{\sf Prod})}(1+|{\sf Ch}(p)|)\Big). Using the fact that ∑p∈𝖡𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽|𝖢𝗁⁡(p)|=O⁡(n)\sum_{p\in{\sf B}_{\sf Prod}}|{\sf Ch}(p)|=O(n), the total time to compute all the value functions is O⁡(n​ 2𝗍𝗐⁡(G𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽))O\big(n\,2^{{\sf tw}(G_{\sf Prod})}\big). Putting everything together, the total running time is O⁡(m​n2​ 2𝗍𝗐⁡(G𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽))O\big(\,m\,n^{2}\,2^{{\sf tw}(G_{\sf Prod})}\,\big).  

In Appendix F, we give a concrete example of how the dynamic programming algorithm in Theorem 4.4 can be applied to compute an optimal assortment for a generalized nested logit model with 1010 products and 77 nests. For this example, the product graph has a treewidth of 22.

5 An FPTAS for Nest Graphs with Bounded Treewidths

A limitation of using the product graph is that the treewidth is lower bounded by the maximum number of products in M^k{\widehat{M}}_{k}; that is, 𝗍𝗐⁡(G𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽)≥maxk∈K⁡|M^k|−1{\sf tw}(G_{\sf Prod})\geq\max_{k\in K}|{\widehat{M}}_{k}|-1. To address this issue, we develop a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) to solve the Aux-Assort problem by considering the tree decomposition over the nest graph, which we denote by 𝖳𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍=(𝖡𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍,𝖤𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍){{\sf T}}_{\sf Nest}=({\sf B}_{\sf Nest},{\sf E}_{\sf Nest}). For any q∈𝖡𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍q\in{\sf B}_{\sf Nest}, the sets Vtcs​(q)\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(q\right), Subt​(q)\textit{{Subt}}\left(q\right), Head​(q)\textit{{Head}}\left(q\right), and Tail​(q)\textit{{Tail}}\left(q\right) now correspond to sets of nests. We first develop some structural properties of the tree decomposition over the nest graph and then introduce a dynamic program. To streamline the discussion, for each Q⊆KQ\subseteq K, let 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽⁡(Q)=⋃k∈QMk{\sf Prod}(Q)=\bigcup_{k\in Q}M_{k} denote all products that belong to at least one nest in QQ.

5.1 Properties of Tree Decomposition over Nest Graph

We present two structural properties of the tree decomposition over the nest graph. The two lemmas are analogous to Lemmas 4.2 and 4.3, and we defer proofs to Appendix C. The first lemma shows that for each q∈𝖡𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍q\in{\sf B}_{\sf Nest} and i∈𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽​(Subt​(q))i\in{\sf Prod}(\textit{{Subt}}\left(q\right)), the set of nests that product ii belongs to, denoted by 𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(i){\sf Nest}(i), must be entirely contained within the subtree rooted at node qq. This ensures that local computations at node qq can be performed without considering nests outside its subtree.

Lemma 5.1 (Subtree and Head Contain All the Relevant Nests)

For each q∈𝖡𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍q\in{\sf B}_{\sf Nest} and i∈𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽​(Subt​(q))i\in{\sf Prod}(\textit{{Subt}}\left(q\right)), we have 𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(i)⊆Subt​(q)∪⋅Head​(q){\sf Nest}(i)\subseteq\textit{{Subt}}\left(q\right)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\textit{{Head}}\left(q\right).

The next lemma shows a separation property for products in 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽​(Subt​(q)){\sf Prod}(\textit{{Subt}}\left(q\right)). A key element in the claim is the set of products defined by {i∈𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽⁡(Tail​(q)):𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(i)⊆Vtcs​(q)}\big\{i\in{\sf Prod}(\textit{{Tail}}\left(q\right)):{\sf Nest}(i)\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(q\right)\big\}, which consists of products that belong to the nests in Tail​(q)\textit{{Tail}}\left(q\right) with the additional requirement that 𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(i){\sf Nest}(i) is fully contained within Vtcs​(q)\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(q\right). In other words, it includes only those products whose associated nests do not extend beyond Vtcs​(q)\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(q\right). We refer to these as the local products of node qq. In the next lemma, we show that 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽​(Subt​(q)){\sf Prod}(\textit{{Subt}}\left(q\right)) can be partitioned into the local products of node qq, and the products that belong to the children nodes of qq. The proof is similar to the proof of Lemma 4.3.

Lemma 5.2 (Separation of Products in a Nest Graph)

For each q∈𝖡𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍q\in{\sf B}_{\sf Nest},

𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽⁡(Subt​(q))={i∈𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽⁡(Tail​(q)):𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(i)⊆Vtcs​(q)}​⋃⋅⁡(⋃⋅a∈𝖢𝗁⁡(q)⁡𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽⁡(Subt​(a))).{\sf Prod}(\textit{{Subt}}\left(q\right))=\big\{i\in{\sf Prod}(\textit{{Tail}}\left(q\right)):{\sf Nest}(i)\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(q\right)\big\}~\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits\Big(\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits_{a\in{\sf Ch}(q)}{\sf Prod}(\textit{{Subt}}\left(a\right))\Big).

Taken together, Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2 establish a strong separation property of the nest graph under tree decomposition. We will use these properties to derive an FPTAS for the Aux-Assort problem.

5.2 Outline of the FPTAS

This section is devoted to providing an overview of the FPTAS based on the tree decomposition of the nest graph. The main result is stated in the following theorem.

Theorem 5.3 (FPTAS)

For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists an algorithm that provides a (1−ϵ)(1-\epsilon)-approximate solution to the Aux-Assort problem with running time O⁡(m2⋅(2​n/ϵ)O⁡(𝗍𝗐⁡(G𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍)))O\Big(~m^{2}\cdot({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{2n/\epsilon}})^{O({\sf tw}(G_{\sf Nest}))}~\Big).

We make two observations. First, Theorems 5.3 and 3.6 yield an FPTAS for the GNL-Assort problem, and 𝗍𝗐⁡(G𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍)≤m{\sf tw}(G_{\sf Nest})\leq m, so the running time of our method is competitive with existing FPTAS in the literature. Second, for the instances of the generalized nested logit model used in Theorems 2.1 and 2.2, we can easily check that the nest graphs have bounded treewidths. Consequently, we have FPTAS available for the instances used in Theorems 2.1 and 2.2. Our FPTAS consists of two main steps: 1) an approximate version of the Aux-Assort problem by restricting to a finite grid, and 2) a dynamic program that exploits the tree decomposition to solve the approximate problem efficiently. We now describe these two steps in more details.

To describe an approximate version of the Aux-Assort problem, for each i∈Ni\in N, define a function θi:ℝ+m→ℝ+\theta_{i}:\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} as follows: for each 𝒔∈ℝ+m\bm{s}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}, θi​(𝒔)=∑k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(i)vi​k​ri/sk1−γk\theta_{i}(\bm{s})=\sum_{k\in{\sf Nest}(i)}v_{ik}r_{i}/s_{k}^{1-\gamma_{k}}. The value θi​(𝒔)\theta_{i}(\bm{s}) corresponds to the contribution of product ii assuming we offer an assortment SS such that Vk​(S)=skV_{k}(S)=s_{k} for k∈𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(i)k\in{\sf Nest}(i). It is easy to verify that the Aux-Assort problem is equivalent to the following:

An Equivalent Formulation of the Aux-Assort Problem:

F∗=maxS⊆N,𝒕∈ℝ+m⁡{∑i∈Sθi​(𝒕):Vk​(S)≤tk​∀k∈K}.F^{*}~=~\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq N,~\bm{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{+}\end{subarray}}\left\{\sum_{i\in S}\theta_{i}(\bm{t})~:~V_{k}(S)\,\leq\,t_{k}~~\forall k\in K\right\}~.

Under the above formulation, we introduce a new set of decision variables that capture the value of Vk​(S)V_{k}(S). The benefit of this approach is that we can linearize the objective function and turn the problem into a knapsack-like problem. However, it also introduces challenges since the vector 𝒕\bm{t} is continuous. To tackle this, we will restrict 𝒕\bm{t} to a finite grid defined as follows. For each accuracy parameter 0<ϵ<10<\epsilon<1 and k∈Kk\in K, define

𝖦𝗋𝗂𝖽k(ϵ)={0}∪⋃j∈Mk{(1+ϵ)ℓ:ℓ=⌊log⁡vj​klog⁡(1+ϵ)⌋,…,⌈log⁡(n​vj​k)log⁡(1+ϵ)⌉},{\sf Grid}_{k}(\epsilon)=\{0\}\cup\bigcup_{j\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{M_{k}}}}\left\{(1+\epsilon)^{\ell}~:~\ell=\bigg\lfloor\frac{\log v_{jk}}{\log(1+\epsilon)}\bigg\rfloor,\dots,\biggl\lceil\frac{\log(nv_{jk})}{\log(1+\epsilon)}\biggr\rceil\right\}~,

and define 𝖦𝗋𝗂𝖽⁡(ϵ)=𝖦𝗋𝗂𝖽1​(ϵ)×⋯×𝖦𝗋𝗂𝖽m​(ϵ){\sf Grid}(\epsilon)={\sf Grid}_{1}(\epsilon)\times\dots\times{\sf Grid}_{m}(\epsilon). By our construction, if S∗S^{*} is an optimal solution to the Aux-Assort problem, we can always find 𝒕∈𝖦𝗋𝗂𝖽\bm{t}\in{\sf Grid} such that tk1+ϵ≤Vk​(S∗)≤tk\frac{t_{k}}{1+\epsilon}\leq V_{k}(S^{*})\leq t_{k} for each k∈Kk\in K. This is because Vk​(S∗)V_{k}(S^{*}) is between vj​kv_{jk} and n​vj​knv_{jk} for some j∈Mkj\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{M_{k}}}, and our construction of 𝖦𝗋𝗂𝖽k​(ϵ){\sf Grid}_{k}(\epsilon) ensures that we discretize the interval [vj​k,n​vj​k][v_{jk},nv_{jk}] in an exponential grid of increment (1+ϵ)(1+\epsilon). Note that the number of values in 𝖦𝗋𝗂𝖽k{\sf Grid}_{k} is O⁡(n​log⁡(n)/ϵ)O\bigl(n\log(n)/\epsilon\bigr).

In addition to restricting 𝒕∈𝖦𝗋𝗂𝖽⁡(ϵ)\bm{t}\in{\sf Grid}(\epsilon), we further round vi​kv_{ik} using a rounding strategy similar to the one used in Désir et al. (2022). We round vi​kv_{ik} to ⌊4​n​vi​kϵ​tk⌋\bigl\lfloor\frac{4nv_{ik}}{\epsilon t_{k}}\bigr\rfloor. Under this rounding strategy, if ∑i∈Svi​k≤tk\sum_{i\in S}v_{ik}\leq t_{k}, then ∑i∈S⌊4​n​vi​kϵ​tk⌋≤⌈4​nϵ⌉\sum_{i\in S}\bigl\lfloor\frac{4nv_{ik}}{\epsilon t_{k}}\bigr\rfloor\leq\bigl\lceil\frac{4n}{\epsilon}\bigr\rceil. Our final reformulation of the Aux-Assort problem becomes

maxS⊆N,𝒕∈𝖦𝗋𝗂𝖽⁡(ϵ)⁡{∑i∈Sθi​(𝒕):∑i∈S⌊4​n​vi​kϵ​tk⌋≤⌈4​nϵ⌉​∀k∈K}.\displaystyle\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq N,~\bm{t}\in{\sf Grid}(\epsilon)\end{subarray}}\left\{\sum_{i\in S}\theta_{i}(\bm{t})~:~\sum_{i\in S}\Big\lfloor\frac{4nv_{ik}}{\epsilon\,t_{k}}\Big\rfloor\leq\Bigl\lceil\frac{4n}{\epsilon}\Bigr\rceil~~\forall k\in K\right\}. (Discretized-Aux-Assort)

The following lemma shows that solving the Discretized-Aux-Assort problem gives a (1−2​ϵ)(1-2\epsilon)-approximate solution to the Aux-Assort problem.

Lemma 5.4

If S^{\widehat{S}} is an optimal solution to the Discretized-Aux-Assort problem, then S^{\widehat{S}} is a (1−2​ϵ)(1-2\epsilon)-approximate solution to the Aux-Assort problem.

The proof of Lemma 5.4 follows arguments similar to those in Désir et al. (2022) and is in Appendix C.3. Note that for each fixed 𝒕\bm{t}, the Discretized-Aux-Assort problem is an mm-dimensional knapsack problem with integer capacity consumption (Fréville 2004), so it can then be solved exactly using a dynamic program. This dynamic program maintains a state variable for each constraint, so the total number of states scales on the order of O⁡((n/ϵ)m)O\!\left((n/\epsilon)^{m}\right), where mm is the number of nests. Enumerating all possible values of 𝒕\bm{t} requires a running time of O⁡(((n/ϵ)​log⁡n)m)O\!\big((\,(n/\epsilon)\log n\,)^{m}\big). Thus, this method has a running time that is exponential in the number of nests. In the next section, we show that by exploiting the tree decomposition of the nest graph, this exponential dependence can be reduced so that the running time is exponential only in the treewidth of the nest graph.

5.3 A Dynamic Program to Solve the Discretized-Aux-Assort Problem

We develop a dynamic program based on the tree decomposition of the nest graph to solve the Discretized-Aux-Assort problem. Motivated by the separation of products in the tree decomposition of the nest graph, we define the following two notations: for each q∈𝖡𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍q\in{\sf B}_{{\sf Nest}},

Nq=𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽⁡(Subt​(q))andN¯q={i∈𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽⁡(Tail​(q)):𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(i)⊆Vtcs​(q)}.N_{q}={\sf Prod}(\textit{{Subt}}\left(q\right))\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\overline{N}}_{q}=\big\{i\in{\sf Prod}(\textit{{Tail}}\left(q\right)):{\sf Nest}(i)\subseteq\textit{{Vtcs}}\left(q\right)\big\}.

Note that N¯q⊆Nq{\overline{N}}_{q}\subseteq N_{q} by Lemma 5.2. We begin by providing some intuition for the dynamic program. Let q∈𝖡𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍q\in{\sf B}_{{\sf Nest}} be a node in the tree decomposition of the nest graph, and let (S^,𝒕^)(\,{\widehat{S}},\widehat{\bm{t}}\,\,) denote an optimal solution to the Discretized-Aux-Assort problem. Our dynamic program proceeds by optimizing the offered products within NqN_{q}. We make two key observations. First, for any i∈S^∩Nqi\in{\widehat{S}}\cap N_{q}, Lemma 5.1 implies that 𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(i)⊆Head​(q)∪⋅Subt​(q){\sf Nest}(i)\subseteq\textit{{Head}}\left(q\right)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\textit{{Subt}}\left(q\right). Hence, to evaluate the contribution of product ii to the objective, it suffices to consider only the nests in Head​(q)∪⋅Subt​(q)\textit{{Head}}\left(q\right)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\textit{{Subt}}\left(q\right).

Second, we distinguish between two types of nests: nests in Subt​(q)\textit{{Subt}}\left(q\right) and nests in Head​(q)\textit{{Head}}\left(q\right). On one hand, if k∈Subt​(q)k\in\textit{{Subt}}\left(q\right), then Mk⊆NqM_{k}\subseteq N_{q}, so (S^∖Nq)∩Mk=∅({\widehat{S}}\setminus N_{q})\cap M_{k}=\varnothing, which implies that vi​k=0v_{ik}=0 for all i∈S^∖Nqi\in{\widehat{S}}\setminus N_{q} and ∑i∈S^∖Nq⌊4​n​vi​kϵ​t^k⌋=0\sum_{i\in{\widehat{S}}\setminus N_{q}}\Big\lfloor\cfrac{4nv_{ik}}{\epsilon\,{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\Big\rfloor=0. The total preference weight for nest kk thus depends only on the products within NqN_{q}. On the other hand, if k∈Head​(q)k\in\textit{{Head}}\left(q\right), then Mk⊈NqM_{k}\not\subseteq N_{q} and it is possible that ∑i∈S^∖Nq⌊4​n​vi​kϵ​t^k⌋>0\sum_{i\in{\widehat{S}}\setminus N_{q}}\Big\lfloor\cfrac{4nv_{ik}}{\epsilon\,{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\Big\rfloor>0, reflecting products that are offered outside of NqN_{q}. Thus, when we optimize locally over NqN_{q}, the preference weight of nests in Head​(q)\textit{{Head}}\left(q\right) also depends on decisions made elsewhere in the tree. These two observations above indicate that, if our goal is to optimize the products offered within NqN_{q}, we must carefully track the information associated with nests in Head​(q)\textit{{Head}}\left(q\right).

For q∈𝖡𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍q\in{\sf B}_{\sf Nest}, let Jq𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍J^{\sf Nest}_{q} denote the value function at node qq of 𝖳𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍{{\sf T}}_{\sf Nest}. The domain of the function Jq𝖭𝖾𝗌𝗍J^{\sf Nest}_{q} is 𝖡𝗎𝖽q×𝖯𝗋𝖾𝖿q{\sf Bud}_{q}\times{\sf Pref}_{q} and the action set is denoted by 𝒜q{\mathcal{A}}_{q}, where 𝖡𝗎𝖽q{\sf Bud}_{q}, 𝖯𝗋𝖾𝖿q{\sf Pref}_{q} and 𝒜q{\mathcal{A}}_{q} are defined by:
